newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China strangles "golden-egg goose" HK-democrat Lee.
newsitem.headline: China strangles "golden-egg goose" HK-democrat Lee.

text.p: Hong Kong democrat Martin Lee accused China on Friday of putting "a noose round the neck of a goose" laying golden eggs, warning Beijing that curbs on Hong Kong freedom could strangle prosperity.
Lee is chairman of the popular Democratic Party, which has the biggest representation in a democratically-elected parliament China is to scrap on July 1, to Western dismay.
"Once upon a time, there was a goose. The goose liked to dance in the morning, fly a bit, and sing in the afternoon," Lee told a business seminar.
"But in the evening, when the sun was setting, when it felt happy...it would lay an egg -- a golden egg," he said.
"Now a new master was about to take over. And he said to the goose: 'Come on, I don't like that.'," Lee said, adding the new master disliked the bird's noise and movement.
"'Sit down, will you?' And to make sure that happened, the new master put a noose round the neck of the goose," Lee said.
The goose continued to lay an egg every day, he said, but "the question is: will the egg remain golden for long?"
China will recover Hong Kong from Britain at midnight on June 30 after 156 years of British colonial rule.
Beijing has announced plans to roll back civil liberties and water down human rights in Hong Kong.

It has also vowed to scrap the present fully-elected Legislative Council upon the handover and replace it with an appointed provisional legislature, chosen by a Beijing-picked panel, that will serve for about a year after the handover.
"I think Hong Kong will be a safe place to invest in, but what I am worried about is long-term prosperity of Hong Kong," Lee said of the territory.
China has promised a 50-year "one-country, two systems" policy that will allow Hong Kong's free-wheeling capitalist system to remain independent of the communist system in the rest of China.
Lee argued Hong Kong must be kept free not only economically but also politically to remain a vibrant economy on the Pacific Rim.
Lack of political freedom could result in a legal system that fails to protect liberties of individuals, including businessmen, he said.
The leading democrat also criticised the provisional legislature, opposed by the colonial administration and democrats in Hong Kong as well as overseas powers including the United States.
The interim chamber's opponents have called it undemocratic.
"How can there be the rule of law to protect freedom without democracy?" Lee said.
"Where do you think the loyalty of those people will lie?" he said, adding the chamber would stand for Beijing instead of Hong Kong people.
He said Hong Kong would lack an independent legal system as the interpretation of key articles of its post-colonial constitution does not lie with local courts but the parliament of China.
Lee was sceptical of Beijing's pledge of a "one country, two systems" policy on Hong Kong.
